title: Πταρμὸς καὶ κλῆσις
titleEn: The Sneeze and the Summons — Odyssey 17.508–606
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Penelope sends Eumaeus to bring the stranger so that she can ask whether he has news of Odysseus. Eumaeus says that the man would enchant her with his tales: he claims to be a guest-friend of Odysseus’s family from Crete and says that Odysseus is alive among the Thesprotians and bringing treasures home. When Telemachus sneezes loudly at her words, Penelope laughs and takes it as a sign that death will come to the suitors; she promises the stranger a cloak and tunic if he tells her the truth. Odysseus, who fears the suitors’ violence, asks through Eumaeus that she wait until sunset, when she can seat him by the fire. Eumaeus brings this back, tells Telemachus to look to his own safety, and goes back to his swine as evening comes on.

sentences.t:
ἔρχεο, δῖ’ Εὔμαιε, κιὼν τὸν ξεῖνον ἄνωχθι
ἐλθέμεν, ὄφρα τί μιν προσπτύξομαι ἠδ’ ἐρέωμαι
εἴ που Ὀδυσσῆος ταλασίφρονος ἠὲ πέπυσται
ἢ ἴδεν ὀφθαλμοῖσι·
sentences.tr:
ercheo, di’ Eumaie, kiōn ton xeinon anōchthi
elthemen, ophra ti min prosptyxomai ēd’ ereōmai
ei pou Odyssēos talasiphronos ēe pepystai
ē iden ophthalmoisi·
sentences.l:
“Go, heavenly Eumaeus, going bid the stranger
to come, so that I may greet him and ask him something,
whether anywhere of enduring-minded Odysseus he has either heard
or has seen with his eyes;
sentences.i: “Go, heavenly Eumaeus, and bid the stranger come, so that I may greet him and ask him something — whether he has heard anything of steadfast Odysseus, or has seen him with his own eyes;
sentences.n: ἔρχεο is a present imperative ‘go’, and ἄνωχθι ‘bid’ is the imperative of ἄνωγα, a perfect that works as a present; κιών ‘going’ adds nothing, so the pair means ‘go and bid’. ἐλθέμεν is an infinitive in -έμεν, ‘to come’. After ὄφρα ‘so that’ the verbs προσπτύξομαι ‘I may greet’ (literally ‘fold myself toward’, so ‘embrace, greet’; a short-vowel subjunctive that looks like a future) and ἐρέωμαι ‘I may ask’ are subjunctives, and both belong to μιν ‘him’. ταλασίφρων is Odysseus’s standing epithet, ‘enduring-minded’. εἴ που … ἠὲ … ἢ is ‘whether anywhere … either … or’; πέπυσται is the perfect of πυνθάνομαι, ‘has heard’, and ἴδεν has no augment (Attic εἶδεν). Ὀδυσσῆος is the epic genitive in -ῆος.

sentences.t: πολυπλάγκτῳ γὰρ ἔοικε.
sentences.tr: polyplanktōi gar eoike.
sentences.l: for to a much-straying one he is like.”
sentences.i: for he looks like a far-roaming man.”
sentences.n: ἔοικε ‘is like, looks like’ takes a dative, here the adjective πολυπλάγκτῳ standing alone for ‘a much-straying man’; the adjective is built on πολύς ‘much’ and the root of πλάζω ‘drive astray’. γάρ gives Penelope’s reason for wanting to question him. The full stop closes her speech.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφης, Εὔμαιε συβῶτα·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ apameibomenos prosephēs, Eumaie sybōta·
sentences.l: Her, answering, you addressed, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.i: In answer you said to her, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.n: The poet turns to speak to Eumaeus: προσέφης is second person, ‘you addressed’, and Εὔμαιε συβῶτα is a vocative, ‘Eumaeus the swineherd’. ἀπαμειβόμενος is ‘answering’ (ἀπό + ἀμείβομαι), and τὴν is the pronoun ‘her’, not the article. συβώτης is built on σῦς ‘swine’ and the root of βόσκω ‘feed’.

sentences.t: εἰ γάρ τοι, βασίλεια, σιωπήσειαν Ἀχαιοί·
sentences.tr: ei gar toi, basileia, siōpēseian Achaioi·
sentences.l: “Would that, queen, the Achaeans were silent for you;
sentences.i: “If only, queen, the Achaeans would fall silent for you;
sentences.n: εἰ γάρ with the optative σιωπήσειαν ‘would be silent’ makes a wish, ‘if only’; what follows from it comes in the next line. τοι is the enclitic dative ‘for you’, and βασίλεια is a vocative, ‘queen’. Ἀχαιοί here means the men in the hall around her, who are the suitors, not the Greeks at Troy.

sentences.t: οἷ’ ὅ γε μυθεῖται, θέλγοιτό κέ τοι φίλον ἦτορ.
sentences.tr: hoi’ ho ge mytheitai, thelgoito ke toi philon ētor.
sentences.l: such things as he tells, would be enchanted, for you, the dear heart.
sentences.i: your heart would be enchanted by the things he tells.
sentences.n: οἷα (elided οἷ’) is ‘such things as’, a neuter plural relative, and ὅ γε is ‘he’ (the pronoun use of ὁ, with γε stressing it). θέλγοιτο κε is an optative with κε, ‘would be enchanted’; θέλγω is ‘enchant, charm’, a word of spells, and it prepares the simile of the singer that follows. τοι is ‘your’ (a dative of the person concerned), and φίλον ἦτορ is ‘dear heart’.

sentences.t:
τρεῖς γὰρ δή μιν νύκτας ἔχον, τρία δ’ ἤματ’ ἔρυξα
ἐν κλισίῃ·
sentences.tr:
treis gar dē min nyktas echon, tria d’ ēmat’ eryxa
en klisiēi·
sentences.l:
For three nights indeed I had him, and three days I kept him
in my hut;
sentences.i: For I kept him with me for three nights and three days in my hut;
sentences.n: ἔχον ‘I had’ is an imperfect without augment (Attic εἶχον), and ἔρυξα ‘I kept’ is the aorist of ἐρύκω ‘hold back, detain’; μιν is ‘him’. The nights are counted before the days. ἤματ’ is ἤματα, ‘days’, and κλισίη ‘hut’ is the swineherd’s own dwelling, here in the dative with ἐν and the Ionic ending -ῃ.

sentences.t: πρῶτον γὰρ ἔμ’ ἵκετο νηὸς ἀποδράς·
sentences.tr: prōton gar em’ hiketo nēos apodras·
sentences.l: for first to me he came, from a ship having run away;
sentences.i: for it was to me that he came first, after running away from a ship;
sentences.n: ἔμ’ is ἐμέ ‘me’, and ἵκετο ‘he came to’ takes a plain accusative. ἀποδράς is the aorist participle of ἀποδιδράσκω ‘run away’, and νηός is the genitive ‘from a ship’. πρῶτον is the adverb ‘first’: he reached Eumaeus before anyone else.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὔ πω κακότητα διήνυσεν ἣν ἀγορεύων.
sentences.tr: all’ ou pō kakotēta diēnysen hēn agoreuōn.
sentences.l: but not yet the misery has he got through, the one he tells of.
sentences.i: but he has not yet reached the end of the misery he describes.
sentences.n: διήνυσεν is the aorist of διανύω ‘bring to the end’, so ‘has not yet finished’, and what is unfinished is his telling of his hardships. The words ἣν ἀγορεύων are compressed: ἥν is the relative ‘which’ (agreeing with κακότητα ‘misery’), and the participle ἀγορεύων ‘telling’ does the work of a verb, giving ‘the misery he tells of’. πω is ‘yet’.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἀοιδὸν ἀνὴρ ποτιδέρκεται, ὅς τε θεῶν ἒξ
ἀείδει δεδαὼς ἔπε’ ἱμερόεντα βροτοῖσι,
τοῦ δ’ ἄμοτον μεμάασιν ἀκουέμεν, ὁππότ’ ἀείδῃ·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hot’ aoidon anēr potiderketai, hos te theōn ex
aeidei dedaōs epe’ himeroenta brotoisi,
tou d’ amoton memaasin akouemen, hoppot’ aeidēi·
sentences.i: As when a man gazes at a singer who sings, taught by the gods, words full of longing for mortals, and they are eager to hear him without ceasing whenever he sings;
sentences.n: ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ opens a simile, ‘and as when’. ποτιδέρκεται is ‘gazes at’ (ποτί = πρός). ὅς τε is a relative with epic τε, ‘the sort who’; ἒξ is the preposition ἐξ ‘from’, set after its noun, so θεῶν ἒξ is ‘from the gods’. δεδαώς is the perfect participle of δάω, ‘having learned’. ἱμερόεντα is ‘full of longing’ (from ἵμερος), words that make listeners long to go on hearing. τοῦ ‘of him’, the singer, depends on ἀκουέμεν ‘to hear’ (infinitive in -έμεν), and μεμάασιν ‘they are eager’ is the perfect of μέμονα; who ‘they’ are is not said. The sense of ἄμοτον is not known; ‘unceasingly’ is the traditional guess. ὁππότ’ is ὁπότε ‘whenever’, and ἀείδῃ is a subjunctive without κε.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐμὲ κεῖνος ἔθελγε παρήμενος ἐν μεγάροισι.
sentences.tr: hōs eme keinos ethelge parēmenos en megaroisi.
sentences.l: so me that man was enchanting, sitting beside me in the halls.
sentences.i: So that man enchanted me, sitting beside me in the hall.
sentences.n: ὡς … ὥς is ‘as … so’: this is the second half of the simile. ἔθελγε is an imperfect, ‘was enchanting’ (θέλγω, as in θέλγοιτο at 514); κεῖνος is ἐκεῖνος ‘that man’, and παρήμενος is ‘sitting beside’. ἐν μεγάροισι is a dative plural in -οισι; the plural ‘halls’ means the one house.

sentences.t:
φησὶ δ’ Ὀδυσσῆος ξεῖνος πατρώϊος εἶναι,
Κρήτῃ ναιετάων, ὅθι Μίνωος γένος ἐστίν.
sentences.tr:
phēsi d’ Odyssēos xeinos patrōïos einai,
Krētēi naietaōn, hothi Minōos genos estin.
sentences.l:
And he says that of Odysseus a guest-friend from his fathers’ time he is,
in Crete dwelling, where of Minos the family is.
sentences.i: He says he is a guest-friend of Odysseus from his fathers’ time, and that he lives in Crete, where the family of Minos is.
sentences.n: φησί ‘he says’ is followed by the infinitive εἶναι ‘that he is’. ξεῖνος here is the guest-friend of a standing bond, and πατρώϊος dates that bond to Odysseus’s fathers, handed down in the family. Κρήτῃ is a dative of place without ἐν, with Ionic -η; ναιετάων is the epic participle of ναιετάω ‘dwell’. γένος is ‘family, stock’, and Μίνωος is the genitive of Minos.

sentences.t:
ἔνθεν δὴ νῦν δεῦρο τόδ’ ἵκετο πήματα πάσχων,
προπροκυλινδόμενος·
sentences.tr:
enthen dē nyn deuro tod’ hiketo pēmata paschōn,
proprokylindomenos·
sentences.l:
From there indeed now here to this place he came, suffering woes,
rolling-himself-onward;
sentences.i: From there he has now come to this place, suffering woes, rolling on and on;
sentences.n: ἔνθεν ‘from there’ ends in -θεν, the ending of motion from; δεῦρο is ‘to here’ and τόδ’ (τόδε) ‘to this place’. ἵκετο is ‘came’, and πήματα πάσχων is ‘suffering woes’. προπροκυλινδόμενος is a middle participle of κυλίνδω ‘roll’ with a doubled προ- ‘forward, forward’: ‘rolling himself onward again and again’, the image of a man tumbled from place to place.

sentences.t:
στεῦται δ’ Ὀδυσῆος ἀκοῦσαι,
ἀγχοῦ, Θεσπρωτῶν ἀνδρῶν ἐν πίονι δήμῳ,
ζωοῦ·
sentences.tr:
steutai d’ Odysēos akousai,
anchou, Thesprōtōn andrōn en pioni dēmōi,
zōou·
sentences.i: He claims to have heard that Odysseus is alive, close by in the rich land of the Thesprotians;
sentences.n: στεῦται is ‘he claims, he declares’ (present of στεῦμαι) and takes the aorist infinitive ἀκοῦσαι ‘to have heard’, whose object is the genitive Ὀδυσῆος, since ἀκούω takes the genitive of the person heard of. ζωοῦ ‘alive’ is also genitive and agrees with Ὀδυσῆος. Ὀδυσῆος is the verse’s other spelling of Ὀδυσσῆος (line 522). ἀγχοῦ is ‘near’; Θεσπρωτῶν ἀνδρῶν ‘the Thesprotian men’ are a people, and ἐν πίονι δήμῳ is ‘in the rich land’ (δῆμος ‘land’, πίων ‘rich, fat’).

sentences.t: πολλὰ δ’ ἄγει κειμήλια ὅνδε δόμονδε.
sentences.tr: polla d’ agei keimēlia honde domonde.
sentences.l: and many treasures he is bringing to his own house.”
sentences.i: and that he is bringing many treasures to his own home.”
sentences.n: The subject changes without warning: ἄγει ‘he is bringing’ is Odysseus, still inside what the stranger claims. κειμήλια are ‘treasures’ kept in store. ὅνδε is the possessive ὅν ‘his own’ with a -δε attached, and δόμονδε has the -δε of direction (δόμον + δε ‘to the house’), so the pair means ‘to his own house’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε περίφρων Πηνελόπεια·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe periphrōn Pēnelopeia·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed circumspect Penelope:
sentences.i: Then circumspect Penelope spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: A reply formula: τὸν is the pronoun ‘him’ (Eumaeus), αὖτε ‘in turn’, and προσέειπε ‘addressed’. περίφρων ‘circumspect’ is Penelope’s standing epithet. The same line opens her next answer at 585.

sentences.t: ἔρχεο, δεῦρο κάλεσσον, ἵν’ ἀντίον αὐτὸς ἐνίσπῃ.
sentences.tr: ercheo, deuro kalesson, hin’ antion autos enispēi.
sentences.l: “Go, here call him, so that face to face himself he may tell.
sentences.i: “Go, call him here, so that he can tell it himself, face to face.
sentences.n: ἔρχεο ‘go’ and κάλεσσον ‘call’ (aorist imperative of καλέω, with -σσ-) are imperatives. ἵνα takes the subjunctive ἐνίσπῃ, ‘so that he may tell’ (from ἐνέπω, aorist ἔνισπον); the Greek gives it no object. ἀντίον is ‘face to face’, and αὐτός ‘himself’.

sentences.t: οὗτοι δ’ ἠὲ θύρῃσι καθήμενοι ἑψιαάσθων.
sentences.tr: houtoi d’ ēe thyrēisi kathēmenoi hepsiaasthōn.
sentences.l: and these men, either at the doors sitting, let them amuse themselves;
sentences.i: As for these men, let them amuse themselves, either sitting at the doors;
sentences.n: οὗτοι ‘these men’ are the suitors, as the next lines show. ἑψιαάσθων is a third-plural imperative, ‘let them amuse themselves’ (ἑψιάομαι), in an uncontracted form. ἠέ … ἢ (next line) is ‘either … or’, and θύρῃσι is a dative plural in -ῃσι, ‘at the doors’.

sentences.t: ἢ αὐτοῦ κατὰ δώματ’, ἐπεί σφισι θυμὸς ἐΰφρων.
sentences.tr: ē autou kata dōmat’, epei sphisi thymos eÿphrōn.
sentences.l: or right here through the house, since to them the heart is cheerful.
sentences.i: or here in the house, since their hearts are cheerful.
sentences.n: αὐτοῦ is the adverb ‘on the spot, right here’, and κατὰ δώματ’ is ‘through the house’. σφισι is ‘to them’. θυμὸς ἐΰφρων is ‘a cheerful heart’: ἐΰφρων ‘of good cheer’ is built on ἐΰ ‘well’ and φρήν. ἐπεί ‘since’ gives the reason they may stay.

sentences.t:
αὐτῶν μὲν γὰρ κτήματ’ ἀκήρατα κεῖτ’ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ,
σῖτος καὶ μέθυ ἡδύ·
sentences.tr:
autōn men gar ktēmat’ akērata keit’ eni oikōi,
sitos kai methy hēdy·
sentences.l:
For of their own indeed the possessions lie untouched in the house,
food and sweet wine;
sentences.i: For their own possessions lie untouched at home, food and sweet wine;
sentences.n: αὐτῶν is ‘their own’ (literally ‘of themselves’), set against ἡμέτερον ‘ours’ two lines later. κεῖτ’ is κεῖται, a singular verb with the neuter plural κτήματα ‘possessions’, as in Attic. ἀκήρατα means ‘untouched, unspoiled’, and ἐνὶ οἴκῳ is ‘in the house’, each man’s own. σῖτος is ‘food’ and μέθυ ἡδύ ‘sweet wine’.

sentences.t: τὰ μὲν οἰκῆες ἔδουσιν,
sentences.tr: ta men oikēes edousin,
sentences.l: these indeed the household servants eat,
sentences.i: their household servants eat those,
sentences.n: τὰ μέν ‘these’ picks up the stores of the previous line, and μέν is answered by οἱ δ’ ‘but they’ in the next unit. οἰκῆες is ‘members of the household, servants’, and ἔδουσιν ‘they eat’ is from ἔδω, the epic form of ἐσθίω. The unit ends at a comma because the sentence runs on for several more lines.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ εἰς ἡμέτερον πωλεύμενοι ἤματα πάντα,
βοῦς ἱερεύοντες καὶ ὄϊς καὶ πίονας αἶγας,
εἰλαπινάζουσιν πίνουσί τε αἴθοπα οἶνον,
μαψιδίως·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ eis hēmeteron pōleumenoi ēmata panta,
bous hiereuontes kai oïs kai pionas aigas,
eilapinazousin pinousi te aithopa oinon,
mapsidiōs·
sentences.l:
but they, to our house going to and fro all the days,
slaughtering oxen and sheep and fat goats,
feast and drink the fire-faced wine,
heedlessly;
sentences.i: Instead they go to and fro in our house every day, slaughtering oxen and sheep and fat goats, and they feast and drink the wine that has the look of fire, heedlessly;
sentences.n: οἱ δ’ ‘but they’ answers τὰ μέν. εἰς ἡμέτερον is ‘to our (house)’ with the noun left out; πωλεύμενοι is ‘going to and fro’, and ἤματα πάντα ‘all the days’ is ‘every day’. βοῦς ἱερεύοντες is ‘slaughtering oxen’: the animals are killed for the suitors’ meals. εἰλαπινάζουσιν is ‘they feast’. αἴθοπα ‘fire-faced’ is built on αἴθω ‘burn’ and ὄψ ‘face, look’, the wine’s colour. μαψιδίως is ‘heedlessly’.

sentences.t: τὰ δὲ πολλὰ κατάνεται.
sentences.tr: ta de polla katanetai.
sentences.l: and the goods, much of them, are wasted away.
sentences.i: and most of our goods are wasted away.
sentences.n: τὰ πολλά is ‘the greater part’ (the article with a neuter plural). κατάνεται is ‘is used up, wasted’; its exact formation is not certain, but the sense is clear from the line.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἔπ’ ἀνήρ,
οἷος Ὀδυσσεὺς ἔσκεν, ἀρὴν ἀπὸ οἴκου ἀμῦναι.
sentences.tr:
ou gar ep’ anēr,
hoios Odysseus esken, arēn apo oikou amynai.
sentences.l:
For there is no man at hand,
such as Odysseus was, to ward ruin off from the house.
sentences.i: For there is no man here like Odysseus to keep ruin from the house.
sentences.n: ἔπ’ is ἔπεστι ‘is there, is at hand’ (the preposition standing for the verb). οἷος … ἔσκεν is ‘such as … was’, with the iterative past form ἔσκεν of εἰμί. ἀρήν here is ‘ruin, bane’ (the same word also means ‘prayer, curse’), and ἀμῦναι is the aorist infinitive of ἀμύνω ‘ward off’. The two spellings Ὀδυσσεύς here and Ὀδυσεύς in the next unit are one name, spelled to fit the verse.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς ἔλθοι καὶ ἵκοιτ’ ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν,
αἶψά κε σὺν ᾧ παιδὶ βίας ἀποτίσεται ἀνδρῶν.
sentences.tr:
ei d’ Odyseus elthoi kai hikoit’ es patrida gaian,
aipsa ke syn hōi paidi bias apotisetai andrōn.
sentences.l:
If Odysseus should come and reach his fatherland,
at once, with his own son, he would exact payment for the violent deeds of the men.”
sentences.i: If Odysseus were to come and reach his fatherland, he would at once, with his own son, exact payment for the men’s violence.”
sentences.n: εἰ with the optatives ἔλθοι and ἵκοιτ’ (ἵκοιτο) is ‘if he should come and reach’; the other half is αἶψά κε with the future ἀποτίσεται, ‘he would exact payment’. σὺν ᾧ παιδί has ᾧ as the possessive ‘his own’ (dative), not the relative. πατρίδα γαῖαν is ‘fatherland’. ἀποτίσεται is a middle future, ‘exact payment’, with βίας ‘violent deeds’ and ἀνδρῶν ‘of the men’, the suitors.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, Τηλέμαχος δὲ μέγ’ ἔπταρεν, ἀμφὶ δὲ δῶμα
σμερδαλέον κονάβησε·
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, Tēlemachos de meg’ eptaren, amphi de dōma
smerdaleon konabēse·
sentences.l:
So she spoke, and Telemachus greatly sneezed, and round about, the house
frightfully resounded;
sentences.i: So she spoke, and Telemachus gave a great sneeze, and the house all round rang out frightfully;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is ‘So she spoke’, here of a woman. μέγ’ is the adverb ‘greatly’, and ἔπταρεν is the aorist of πταίρω (also πτάρνυμαι) ‘sneeze’. ἀμφί is an adverb ‘round about’, and δῶμα ‘house’ is the subject of κονάβησε, the aorist of κοναβέω ‘ring, resound’; σμερδαλέον, a neuter adjective used as an adverb, is ‘frightfully’. Penelope reads this sneeze as a sign in her next speech.

sentences.t:
γέλασσε δὲ Πηνελόπεια,
αἶψα δ’ ἄρ’ Εὔμαιον ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
gelasse de Pēnelopeia,
aipsa d’ ar’ Eumaion epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
and she laughed, Penelope,
and at once then, to Eumaeus, winged words she spoke:
sentences.i: Penelope laughed, and at once she spoke winged words to Eumaeus:
sentences.n: γέλασσε is the aorist of γελάω ‘laugh’ with the epic doubled σ; the Greek does not say why she laughs. The second line is a standing formula: ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’ and προσηύδα ‘spoke to’, with the name Εὔμαιον in the accusative, ‘to Eumaeus’.

sentences.t: ἔρχεό μοι, τὸν ξεῖνον ἐναντίον ὧδε κάλεσσον.
sentences.tr: ercheo moi, ton xeinon enantion hōde kalesson.
sentences.l: “Go for me, the stranger face to face here call.
sentences.i: “Go, call the stranger here before me.
sentences.n: ἔρχεό is ἔρχεο ‘go’ with its accent changed by the following enclitic μοι ‘for me’ (a dative of the person concerned). ἐναντίον is ‘face to face, before (me)’, ὧδε is ‘here’, and κάλεσσον ‘call’ is the imperative of line 529: she gives her order again, now that the sign has come.

sentences.t: οὐχ ὁράᾳς ὅ μοι υἱὸς ἐπέπταρε πᾶσιν ἔπεσσι;
sentences.tr: ouch horaāis ho moi huios epeptare pasin epessi;
sentences.l: Do you not see that my son sneezed at all the words?
sentences.i: Do you not see that my son sneezed at all the words?
sentences.n: ὁράᾳς is ὁρᾷς ‘you see’ in an uncontracted form. ὅ is the neuter relative used as ‘that’, and μοι ‘my’ (dative of the possessor) goes with υἱός ‘son’. ἐπέπταρε is the aorist of ἐπιπταίρω (also ἐπιπτάρνυμαι) ‘sneeze at’, with the dative πᾶσιν ἔπεσσι ‘at all the words’ (dative plural in -εσσι). A sneeze after a statement was taken as a sign that it would come true; the next lines say what she draws from it.

sentences.t:
τῷ κε καὶ οὐκ ἀτελὴς θάνατος μνηστῆρσι γένοιτο
πᾶσι μάλ’, οὐδέ κέ τις θάνατον καὶ κῆρας ἀλύξει.
sentences.tr:
tōi ke kai ouk atelēs thanatos mnēstērsi genoito
pasi mal’, oude ke tis thanaton kai kēras alyxei.
sentences.l:
Therefore too would death not be unfulfilled for the suitors,
for all of them indeed, nor would any escape death and the death-fates.
sentences.i: So death would not fail of its fulfilment for the suitors, for every one of them, and no one would escape death and the spirits of death.
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘therefore’ (a case of ὁ used as an adverb), and καί is ‘too’. γένοιτο is an optative with κε, ‘would come to be’, and ἀλύξει is a future ‘will escape’ also used with κε. οὐκ ἀτελής ‘not unfulfilled’ is a litotes: the death will certainly be carried out. μνηστῆρσι is a dative plural in -ῆρσι. θάνατον καὶ κῆρας: κήρ is a power that brings death, ‘death-fate’, here in the plural.

sentences.t: ἄλλο δέ τοι ἐρέω, σὺ δ’ ἐνὶ φρεσὶ βάλλεο σῇσιν·
sentences.tr: allo de toi ereō, sy d’ eni phresi balleo sēisin·
sentences.l: And another thing to you I will say, and you in your own mind lay it:
sentences.i: And I will tell you something else; lay it up in your own mind:
sentences.n: ἄλλο … τοι ἐρέω is ‘I will tell you something else’ (ἐρέω is a future of ‘say’; τοι is ‘to you’). βάλλεο is a middle imperative, ‘lay (it)’, and σῇσιν is the possessive σός in a dative plural in -ῃσιν, ‘your own’, agreeing with φρεσί ‘mind’.

sentences.t:
αἴ κ’ αὐτὸν γνώω νημερτέα πάντ’ ἐνέποντα,
ἕσσω μιν χλαῖνάν τε χιτῶνά τε, εἵματα καλά.
sentences.tr:
ai k’ auton gnōō nēmertea pant’ eneponta,
hessō min chlainan te chitōna te, heimata kala.
sentences.l:
If I come to know him telling all things unerringly,
I will clothe him in a cloak and a tunic, fine clothes.”
sentences.i: If I find that he tells me everything unerringly, I will clothe him in a cloak and a tunic, fine clothes.”
sentences.n: αἴ κ’ is εἰ κε ‘if’ in its epic form, and γνώω is the aorist subjunctive of γιγνώσκω ‘come to know, recognise’ (Attic γνῶ). ἐνέποντα is ‘telling’, with νημερτέα πάντ’ ‘everything unerringly’. ἕσσω is the future of ἕννυμι ‘clothe’, with μιν ‘him’ and the garments χλαῖνα ‘cloak’ and χιτών ‘tunic’; εἵματα καλά ‘fine clothes’ restates them.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, βῆ δὲ συφορβός, ἐπεὶ τὸν μῦθον ἄκουσεν·
sentences.tr: hōs phato, bē de syphorbos, epei ton mython akousen·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and went the swineherd, when the word he heard;
sentences.i: So she spoke, and the swineherd went, when he had heard the word;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is ‘So she spoke’. βῆ is the unaugmented aorist ‘went’ (Attic ἔβη). συφορβός ‘swineherd’ is built on σῦς ‘swine’ and φέρβω ‘feed’, and it is another name for Eumaeus. τὸν μῦθον is ‘the word, the speech’; ἄκουσεν is ‘heard’.

sentences.t: ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱστάμενος ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: anchou d’ histamenos epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l: and standing close by, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: and, standing close beside him, spoke winged words:
sentences.n: ἀγχοῦ is ‘close by’, and ἱστάμενος is the present middle participle ‘standing’. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the formula ‘spoke winged words’; it brings in Eumaeus’s speech to the stranger.

sentences.t:
ξεῖνε πάτερ, καλέει σε περίφρων Πηνελόπεια,
μήτηρ Τηλεμάχοιο·
sentences.tr:
xeine pater, kaleei se periphrōn Pēnelopeia,
mētēr Tēlemachoio·
sentences.l:
“Stranger, father, calls you circumspect Penelope,
the mother of Telemachus;
sentences.i: “Stranger, father, circumspect Penelope is calling you, the mother of Telemachus;
sentences.n: ξεῖνε πάτερ is a respectful address to an older stranger, ‘stranger, father’; πάτερ claims no kinship. καλέει is the uncontracted form of καλεῖ ‘calls’, and σε is ‘you’. περίφρων ‘circumspect’ is Penelope’s standing epithet, and μήτηρ Τηλεμάχοιο ‘mother of Telemachus’ (genitive in -οιο) stands in apposition to her name.

sentences.t:
μεταλλῆσαί τί ἑ θυμὸς
ἀμφὶ πόσει κέλεται, καὶ κήδεά περ πεπαθυίῃ.
sentences.tr:
metallēsai ti he thymos
amphi posei keletai, kai kēdea per pepathuiēi.
sentences.l:
to inquire something her heart bids her
about her husband, even though she has suffered sorrows.
sentences.i: her heart urges her to ask something about her husband, even though she has suffered sorrows.
sentences.n: μεταλλῆσαι is the aorist infinitive of μεταλλάω ‘inquire’; ἑ is ‘her’ (accusative), θυμός ‘heart’, and κέλεται ‘bids, urges’ (κέλομαι). ἀμφὶ πόσει is ‘about her husband’ (ἀμφί with the dative; πόσις ‘husband’). καὶ … περ is ‘even though’, with πεπαθυίῃ, the perfect participle of πάσχω ‘having suffered’, and κήδεα ‘sorrows’. The participle is dative where the accusative ἑ might be expected, but the sense is clear: she has suffered griefs and still wants to ask.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κέ σε γνώῃ νημερτέα πάντ’ ἐνέποντα,
ἕσσει σε χλαῖνάν τε χιτῶνά τε, τῶν σὺ μάλιστα
χρηΐζεις·
sentences.tr:
ei de ke se gnōēi nēmertea pant’ eneponta,
hessei se chlainan te chitōna te, tōn sy malista
chrēïzeis·
sentences.i: But if she finds that you tell her everything unerringly, she will clothe you in a cloak and a tunic, which you need most;
sentences.n: εἰ … κε with the aorist subjunctive γνώῃ ‘comes to know’ is followed by the future ἕσσει ‘she will clothe’. χρηΐζεις ‘you need’ takes the genitive, so τῶν is the relative ‘of which’, not the article. Eumaeus repeats Penelope’s promise without the words ‘fine clothes’.

sentences.t:
σῖτον δὲ καὶ αἰτίζων κατὰ δῆμον
γαστέρα βοσκήσεις·
sentences.tr:
siton de kai aitizōn kata dēmon
gastera boskēseis·
sentences.l:
and food, even begging through the land,
your belly you will feed;
sentences.i: and you will feed your belly on food, even by begging through the land;
sentences.n: αἰτίζων is a participle ‘begging’ with the object σῖτον ‘food’, and καί marks it as ‘even’. κατὰ δῆμον is ‘through the land’ (δῆμος ‘land, district’). γαστέρα βοσκήσεις is ‘you will feed your belly’ (βόσκω ‘feed’), a blunt word for the stomach.

sentences.t: δώσει δέ τοι ὅς κ’ ἐθέλῃσι.
sentences.tr: dōsei de toi hos k’ ethelēisi.
sentences.l: and will give to you whoever may wish.”
sentences.i: and whoever wishes will give to you.”
sentences.n: δώσει ‘will give’ has no stated subject; the relative clause ὅς κ’ ἐθέλῃσι ‘whoever may wish’ supplies it (ἐθέλῃσι is a subjunctive in -σι). τοι is ‘to you’. This closes Eumaeus’s message.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe polytlas dios Odysseus·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: The reply formula of 528, now with Odysseus as speaker: τὸν ‘him’ is Eumaeus. πολύτλας ‘much-enduring’ and δῖος ‘heavenly’ are the standing epithets with his name.

sentences.t:
Εὔμαι’, αἶψά κ’ ἐγὼ νημερτέα πάντ’ ἐνέποιμι
κούρῃ Ἰκαρίοιο, περίφρονι Πηνελοπείῃ·
sentences.tr:
Eumai’, aipsa k’ egō nēmertea pant’ enepoimi
kourēi Ikarioio, periphroni Pēnelopeiēi·
sentences.l:
“Eumaeus, at once I would tell all things unerringly
to the daughter of Icarius, to circumspect Penelope;
sentences.i: “Eumaeus, I would tell the daughter of Icarius, circumspect Penelope, everything unerringly at once;
sentences.n: Εὔμαι’ is the vocative Εὔμαιε with its ending elided. αἶψά κε … ἐνέποιμι is an optative with κε, ‘I would tell’; νημερτέα πάντ’ is ‘everything unerringly’. κούρῃ is ‘to the daughter’ (κούρη ‘daughter’ here), Ἰκαρίοιο is the genitive of Icarius, and περίφρονι Πηνελοπείῃ is the dative of Penelope with her epithet.

sentences.t: οἶδα γὰρ εὖ περὶ κείνου, ὁμὴν δ’ ἀνεδέγμεθ’ ὀϊζύν.
sentences.tr: oida gar eu peri keinou, homēn d’ anedegmeth’ oïzyn.
sentences.l: for I know well about that man, and the same distress we have taken upon ourselves.
sentences.i: For I know him well, and we have borne the same distress.
sentences.n: κείνου is ἐκείνου ‘that man’, with περί ‘about’: Odysseus, the stranger, is speaking of Odysseus in the third person. ὁμήν is ὁμός ‘the same, shared’, agreeing with ὀϊζύν ‘distress’ (accusative). ἀνεδέγμεθ’ is a past tense of ἀναδέχομαι ‘take upon oneself, endure’, with the final -α elided.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ μνηστήρων χαλεπῶν ὑποδείδι’ ὅμιλον,
τῶν ὕβρις τε βίη τε σιδήρεον οὐρανὸν ἵκει.
sentences.tr:
alla mnēstērōn chalepōn hypodeidi’ homilon,
tōn hybris te biē te sidēreon ouranon hikei.
sentences.l:
But I fear the throng of harsh suitors,
whose both insolence and violence the iron heaven reaches.
sentences.i: But I fear the throng of harsh suitors, whose insolence and violence reach the iron sky.
sentences.n: ὑποδείδι’ is ὑποδείδια ‘I fear, am afraid of’, a perfect with present sense, and it takes the accusative ὅμιλον ‘throng’; χαλεπῶν is ‘harsh’. τῶν is the relative ‘whose’. ὕβρις τε βίη τε is ‘both insolence and violence’. σιδήρεον οὐρανόν, ‘the iron heaven’, pictures the sky as a hard vault; the words say that the suitors’ arrogance has reached as high as it can go.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ νῦν, ὅτε μ’ οὗτος ἀνὴρ κατὰ δῶμα κιόντα
οὔ τι κακὸν ῥέξαντα βαλὼν ὀδύνῃσιν ἔδωκεν,
οὔτε τι Τηλέμαχος τό γ’ ἐπήρκεσεν οὔτε τις ἄλλος.
sentences.tr:
kai gar nyn, hote m’ houtos anēr kata dōma kionta
ou ti kakon rhexanta balōn odynēisin edōken,
oute ti Tēlemachos to g’ epērkesen oute tis allos.
sentences.l:
For even now, when this man, as I went through the house,
having done no evil at all, struck me and gave me over to pains,
neither did Telemachus ward that off, nor anyone else.
sentences.i: For even now, when this man struck me as I was going through the house, though I had done no harm, and gave me over to pain, neither Telemachus nor anyone else warded it off.
sentences.n: καὶ γὰρ νῦν ‘for even now’ brings the proof of his fear, the blow he has just had. ὅτε begins a clause whose subject is οὗτος ἀνήρ ‘this man’, who is not named; κιόντα ‘going’ and ῥέξαντα ‘having done’ (aorist of ῥέζω) agree with μ’ ‘me’, and βαλών ‘having struck’ is the man’s act, with ὀδύνῃσιν ἔδωκεν ‘gave over to pains’. The main clause is οὔτε … οὔτε ‘neither … nor’: ἐπήρκεσεν is the aorist of ἐπαρκέω ‘ward off’, τό γ’ is ‘that’, and τι is ‘at all’.

sentences.t:
τῷ νῦν Πηνελόπειαν ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἄνωχθι
μεῖναι, ἐπειγομένην περ, ἐς ἠέλιον καταδύντα·
sentences.tr:
tōi nyn Pēnelopeian eni megaroisin anōchthi
meinai, epeigomenēn per, es ēelion katadynta·
sentences.l:
Therefore now Penelope in the halls bid
to wait, though she is eager, until the sun has set;
sentences.i: So now bid Penelope wait in the halls, eager as she is, until the sun has set;
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘therefore’, and ἄνωχθι ‘bid’ (as in line 508) takes the infinitive μεῖναι ‘to wait’, with Πηνελόπειαν as its accusative subject and ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ‘in the halls’. ἐπειγομένην περ is ‘though she is pressing on’, that is, eager. ἐς ἠέλιον καταδύντα is ‘until the sun has set’ (literally ‘to the sun having set’; καταδύντα is the aorist participle of καταδύω ‘go down, set’).

sentences.t:
καὶ τότε μ’ εἰρέσθω πόσιος πέρι νόστιμον ἦμαρ,
ἀσσοτέρω καθίσασα παραὶ πυρί·
sentences.tr:
kai tote m’ eiresthō posios peri nostimon ēmar,
assoterō kathisasa parai pyri·
sentences.l:
and then let her ask me, about her husband, the homecoming day,
having seated (me) nearer, beside the fire;
sentences.i: and then let her ask me about the day of her husband’s homecoming, when she has seated me nearer, beside the fire;
sentences.n: εἰρέσθω is the aorist imperative of ἔρομαι ‘ask’, ‘let her ask’; it takes two accusatives, μ’ ‘me’ and νόστιμον ἦμαρ ‘the homecoming day’, and πόσιος πέρι is ‘about her husband’ (πέρι follows its noun, = περὶ πόσιος). καθίσασα is the aorist participle of καθίζω ‘seat’, used transitively: ‘having seated (me)’. ἀσσοτέρω is the comparative adverb ‘nearer’, and παραί is παρά with the dative, ‘beside’.

sentences.t:
εἵματα γάρ τοι
λύγρ’ ἔχω·
sentences.tr:
heimata gar toi
lygr’ echō·
sentences.l:
for clothes, you see,
grievous I have;
sentences.i: for, you see, I have grievous clothes;
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason he asks to sit by the fire: his clothes are poor. τοι is the particle ‘you see’ (it could also be the dative ‘to you’). λύγρ’ is λυγρά ‘grievous’, neuter plural agreeing with εἵματα ‘clothes’, and ἔχω is ‘I have, I wear’.

sentences.t: οἶσθα καὶ αὐτός, ἐπεί σε πρῶθ’ ἱκέτευσα.
sentences.tr: oistha kai autos, epei se prōth’ hiketeusa.
sentences.l: you know it also yourself, since you first I supplicated.”
sentences.i: you know it yourself, since it was to you that I first made my plea as a suppliant.”
sentences.n: οἶσθα ‘you know’ is the perfect of οἶδα with present sense, and καὶ αὐτός is ‘yourself as well’. ἱκέτευσα is the aorist of ἱκετεύω, ‘I made my plea as a suppliant’; πρῶθ’ is πρῶτα ‘first’, so Eumaeus was the first man he approached.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, βῆ δὲ συφορβός, ἐπεὶ τὸν μῦθον ἄκουσε.
sentences.tr: hōs phato, bē de syphorbos, epei ton mython akouse.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and went the swineherd, when the word he heard.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the swineherd went, when he had heard the word.
sentences.n: The closing formula of 551, now after a man’s speech: ὣς φάτο is ‘So he spoke’. ἄκουσε and ἄκουσεν are one form, the final -ν being optional.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ὑπὲρ οὐδοῦ βάντα προσηύδα Πηνελόπεια·
sentences.tr: ton d’ hyper oudou banta prosēuda Pēnelopeia·
sentences.l: And him, as he stepped over the threshold, Penelope addressed:
sentences.i: And Penelope spoke to him as he stepped over the threshold:
sentences.n: τὸν is ‘him’, Eumaeus. ὑπὲρ οὐδοῦ βάντα is ‘having stepped over the threshold’ (ὑπέρ with the genitive οὐδοῦ; βάντα is the aorist participle of βαίνω), so he has just come back into the hall. προσηύδα is ‘addressed’.

sentences.t: οὐ σύ γ’ ἄγεις, Εὔμαιε·
sentences.tr: ou sy g’ ageis, Eumaie·
sentences.l: “You, at least, are not bringing him, Eumaeus;
sentences.i: “You are not bringing him, Eumaeus;
sentences.n: οὐ σύ γ’ ἄγεις is ‘you are not bringing (him)’; γε stresses σύ, ‘you, at least’. The Greek has no word for ‘him’: Eumaeus has come back alone.

sentences.t: τί τοῦτ’ ἐνόησεν ἀλήτης;
sentences.tr: ti tout’ enoēsen alētēs;
sentences.l: what has the vagrant thought in this?
sentences.i: What did the vagrant have in mind by this?
sentences.n: ἐνόησεν is the aorist of νοέω ‘perceive, think’. τί … τοῦτ’ is literally ‘what in this?’, an accusative of respect: ‘what did he have in mind in this matter?’. ἀλήτης is ‘vagrant’ (from ἀλάομαι ‘wander’).

sentences.t:
ἦ τινά που δείσας ἐξαίσιον ἦε καὶ ἄλλως
αἰδεῖται κατὰ δῶμα;
sentences.tr:
ē tina pou deisas exaision ēe kai allōs
aideitai kata dōma;
sentences.l:
Can it be that, someone having feared, perhaps, outrageous, or even otherwise,
he is shy in the house?
sentences.i: Can it be that he has feared someone outrageous, or is he shy in the house for some other reason?
sentences.n: ἦ opens a question, ‘can it be that’. δείσας is the aorist participle of δείδω ‘fear’; τινά is ‘someone’, and ἐξαίσιον ‘beyond what is due, outrageous’ (from ἐξ and αἶσα ‘portion’) agrees with it, though it could also be read as an adverb, ‘excessively’. που is ‘perhaps’, and ἦε καὶ ἄλλως is ‘or even otherwise’, that is, for some other reason. αἰδεῖται, from αἰδέομαι, is ‘feels shame, is shy’; κατὰ δῶμα is ‘in the house’. The Greek question mark ends the unit.

sentences.t: κακὸς δ’ αἰδοῖος ἀλήτης.
sentences.tr: kakos d’ aidoios alētēs.
sentences.l: and bad is a shamefaced vagrant.”
sentences.i: and a shamefaced vagrant is no good.”
sentences.n: A saying with no verb: ‘and a shamefaced vagrant is a bad thing’. αἰδοῖος is built on αἰδώς ‘shame, respect’; it often means ‘revered’, but here it describes the man who feels shame, ‘shamefaced’, and κακός ‘bad’ means worthless: a beggar who is shy does himself no good.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφης, Εὔμαιε συβῶτα·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ apameibomenos prosephēs, Eumaie sybōta·
sentences.l: Her, answering, you addressed, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.i: In answer you said to her, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.n: The same formula as at 512: the poet again speaks to Eumaeus in the second person, προσέφης ‘you addressed’, with the vocative Εὔμαιε συβῶτα.

sentences.t:
μυθεῖται κατὰ μοῖραν, ἅ πέρ κ’ οἴοιτο καὶ ἄλλος,
ὕβριν ἀλυσκάζων ἀνδρῶν ὑπερηνορεόντων.
sentences.tr:
mytheitai kata moiran, ha per k’ oioito kai allos,
hybrin alyskazōn andrōn hyperēnoreontōn.
sentences.l:
“He speaks according to what is fitting, such things as another too would suppose,
avoiding the insolence of men over-bold.
sentences.i: “He speaks as is fitting, what any other man would think too, shunning the insolence of overbearing men.
sentences.n: μυθεῖται is ‘he speaks’ (the stranger). κατὰ μοῖραν is ‘as is fitting’, literally ‘according to portion’. ἅ πέρ κ’ οἴοιτο is ‘such things as … would suppose’, an optative with κε, and καὶ ἄλλος is ‘any other man too’. ἀλυσκάζων is a participle of ἀλυσκάζω ‘keep avoiding’, with ὕβριν ‘insolence’ as its object, and ὑπερηνορεόντων ‘over-bold’ (built on ὑπέρ and ἠνορέη ‘manliness’) agrees with ἀνδρῶν ‘men’.

sentences.t: ἀλλά σε μεῖναι ἄνωγεν ἐς ἠέλιον καταδύντα.
sentences.tr: alla se meinai anōgen es ēelion katadynta.
sentences.l: But you he bids to wait until the sun has set.
sentences.i: But he bids you wait until the sun has set.
sentences.n: ἄνωγεν is the third person of ἄνωγα ‘bid’ (compare ἄνωχθι at 508), followed by the infinitive μεῖναι ‘to wait’. ἐς ἠέλιον καταδύντα is ‘until the sun has set’, as at 570.

sentences.t:
καὶ δὲ σοὶ ὧδ’ αὐτῇ πολὺ κάλλιον, ὦ βασίλεια,
οἴην πρὸς ξεῖνον φάσθαι ἔπος ἠδ’ ἐπακοῦσαι.
sentences.tr:
kai de soi hōd’ autēi poly kallion, ō basileia,
oiēn pros xeinon phasthai epos ēd’ epakousai.
sentences.l:
And also for you yourself thus it is much finer, O queen,
alone with the stranger to speak a word and to listen.”
sentences.i: And it is much better for you yourself, queen, to speak with the stranger alone and to hear what he says.”
sentences.n: καὶ δέ is ‘and also, moreover’; σοὶ … αὐτῇ is ‘for you yourself’, and ὧδ’ is ‘in this way’. κάλλιον is the comparative of καλός, ‘finer, better’, with πολύ ‘much’. ὦ βασίλεια is a vocative, ‘O queen’. οἴην ‘alone’ is a feminine accusative agreeing with the unexpressed ‘you’ that is the subject of the infinitives φάσθαι ‘to speak’ (from φημί) and ἐπακοῦσαι ‘to listen’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε περίφρων Πηνελόπεια·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe periphrōn Pēnelopeia·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed circumspect Penelope:
sentences.i: Then circumspect Penelope spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: The same line as 528, now answering Eumaeus’s report: τὸν ‘him’ is Eumaeus, and the formula runs ‘him then in turn addressed’.

sentences.t: οὐκ ἄφρων ὁ ξεῖνος·
sentences.tr: ouk aphrōn ho xeinos·
sentences.l: “Not senseless the stranger;
sentences.i: “The stranger is not senseless;
sentences.n: ἄφρων is ἀ- ‘not’ and φρήν ‘mind’, ‘senseless’, with the verb ‘is’ left out. ὁ ξεῖνος is ‘the stranger’, with ὁ close to the article.

sentences.t: ὀΐεται, ὥς περ ἂν εἴη·
sentences.tr: oïetai, hōs per an eiē·
sentences.l: he supposes, just as it may be;
sentences.i: he supposes things to be just as they may be;
sentences.n: ὀΐεται is from ὀΐομαι ‘suppose, expect’ (Attic οἴομαι). ὥς περ ἂν εἴη is ‘just as it might be’, an optative with ἄν: he reckons matters as they really stand.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ πού τινες ὧδε καταθνητῶν ἀνθρώπων
ἀνέρες ὑβρίζοντες ἀτάσθαλα μηχανόωνται.
sentences.tr:
ou gar pou tines hōde katathnētōn anthrōpōn
aneres hybrizontes atasthala mēchanoōntai.
sentences.l:
For not anywhere do any thus, of mortal humans,
men, being insolent, devise wanton things.”
sentences.i: For nowhere do men among mortal humans, acting insolently, devise such wanton deeds.”
sentences.n: οὐ … τινες is ‘not any’, and πού is ‘anywhere’. ὧδε ‘thus’ points to the suitors’ conduct just spoken of. καταθνητῶν is a poetic form of θνητῶν ‘mortal’; ἀνέρες is ‘men’, ὑβρίζοντες ‘acting insolently’ (from ὕβρις), and ἀτάσθαλα ‘wanton things’ is a neuter plural. μηχανόωνται ‘devise’ is the stretched, uncontracted form of μηχανῶνται.

sentences.t:
ἡ μὲν ἄρ’ ὣς ἀγόρευεν, ὁ δ’ ᾤχετο δῖος ὑφορβὸς
μνηστήρων ἐς ὅμιλον, ἐπεὶ διεπέφραδε πάντα.
sentences.tr:
hē men ar’ hōs agoreuen, ho d’ ōicheto dios hyphorbos
mnēstērōn es homilon, epei diepephrade panta.
sentences.l:
She, then, so spoke, and he went off, the heavenly swineherd,
to the throng of the suitors, when he had made everything plain.
sentences.i: She spoke in this way, and the heavenly swineherd went off into the throng of the suitors, when he had made everything plain.
sentences.n: ἡ μὲν … ὁ δέ is ‘she … but he’, the pronoun use of ἡ and ὁ. ἀγόρευεν is an imperfect, ‘spoke’. ᾤχετο is ‘went off’ (οἴχομαι), and δῖος ὑφορβός is ‘the heavenly swineherd’ (ὑφορβός from ὑπό and φέρβω ‘feed’, another name for Eumaeus). διεπέφραδε is the aorist of διαφράζω ‘make plain, explain fully’, with πάντα ‘everything’.

sentences.t:
αἶψα δὲ Τηλέμαχον ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα,
ἄγχι σχὼν κεφαλήν, ἵνα μὴ πευθοίαθ’ οἱ ἄλλοι·
sentences.tr:
aipsa de Tēlemachon epea pteroenta prosēuda,
anchi schōn kephalēn, hina mē peuthoiath’ hoi alloi·
sentences.l:
And at once, to Telemachus, winged words he spoke,
holding his head close, so that the others should not hear:
sentences.i: At once he spoke winged words to Telemachus, holding his head close so that the others should not hear:
sentences.n: The same formula as at 543 (there with ἄρ’ after αἶψα δ’), now with Τηλέμαχον ‘Telemachus’ in the accusative. ἄγχι σχών is the aorist participle of ἔχω with ἄγχι ‘near’, ‘bringing close’, and κεφαλήν ‘head’ is its object. ἵνα μή ‘so that not’ takes the optative πευθοίαθ’ (πευθοίατο, third plural of πεύθομαι ‘learn, hear’), as a purpose clause after a past verb. οἱ ἄλλοι is ‘the others’.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλ’, ἐγὼ μὲν ἄπειμι, σύας καὶ κεῖνα φυλάξων,
σὸν καὶ ἐμὸν βίοτον·
sentences.tr:
ō phil’, egō men apeimi, syas kai keina phylaxōn,
son kai emon bioton·
sentences.l:
“O friend, I for my part am going away, to guard the swine and those things,
your livelihood and mine;
sentences.i: “My friend, I am going away to guard the swine and the rest — your livelihood and mine;
sentences.n: ὦ φίλ’ is a vocative, ‘O friend’ (φίλε with its ending elided). ἄπειμι is ‘I am going away’ (ἀπό + εἶμι ‘go’), with ἐγὼ μέν ‘I for my part’. φυλάξων is a future participle of purpose, ‘to guard’. κεῖνα is ἐκεῖνα ‘those things’, and σὸν καὶ ἐμὸν βίοτον ‘your livelihood and mine’ stands in apposition to σύας καὶ κεῖνα; βίοτος is ‘means of living’.

sentences.t: σοὶ δ’ ἐνθάδε πάντα μελόντων.
sentences.tr: soi d’ enthade panta melontōn.
sentences.l: and to you let all things here be a care.
sentences.i: but let everything here be your concern.
sentences.n: σοὶ δέ ‘but to you’ answers ἐγὼ μέν. μελόντων is a third-plural imperative of μέλω, ‘let them be a care (to you)’, and ἐνθάδε is ‘here’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸν μέν σε πρῶτα σάω, καὶ φράζεο θυμῷ
μή τι πάθῃς·
sentences.tr:
auton men se prōta saō, kai phrazeo thymōi
mē ti pathēis·
sentences.l:
Yourself, first, keep safe, and take thought in your heart
lest you suffer anything;
sentences.i: First of all keep yourself safe, and take care in your heart that no harm comes to you;
sentences.n: σάω is an imperative ‘keep safe’, from σαόω, an older form of σῴζω ‘save’; αὐτὸν … σε is ‘yourself’, and πρῶτα ‘first’. φράζεο is a middle imperative, ‘consider, take care’, and μή with the aorist subjunctive πάθῃς ‘lest you suffer’ says what to guard against. θυμῷ is a dative, ‘in your heart’.

sentences.t:
πολλοὶ δὲ κακὰ φρονέουσιν Ἀχαιῶν,
τοὺς Ζεὺς ἐξολέσειε πρὶν ἡμῖν πῆμα γενέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
polloi de kaka phroneousin Achaiōn,
tous Zeus exoleseie prin hēmin pēma genesthai.
sentences.l:
and many of the Achaeans think evil things,
whom Zeus may utterly destroy before woe comes to us.”
sentences.i: and many of the Achaeans mean evil — may Zeus destroy them utterly before woe comes upon us.”
sentences.n: πολλοὶ … Ἀχαιῶν is ‘many of the Achaeans’ (a partitive genitive), the Achaeans being the men in the hall. κακὰ φρονέουσιν is ‘think evil things’, with an uncontracted verb. τοὺς is the relative ‘whom’, and ἐξολέσειε is an optative of wish, ‘may he destroy utterly’ (ἐξ- intensifies ὄλλυμι). πρὶν … γενέσθαι is ‘before … comes to be’, an infinitive after πρίν; πῆμα is ‘woe’, and ἡμῖν ‘to us’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: Telemachus’s reply formula: τὸν ‘him’ is Eumaeus, αὖ ‘in turn’, and ηὔδα ‘spoke’. πεπνυμένος ‘prudent’ is his standing epithet, and ἀντίον is ‘face to face’.

sentences.t: ἔσσεται οὕτως, ἄττα·
sentences.tr: essetai houtōs, atta·
sentences.l: “It shall be so, father;
sentences.i: “So it shall be, father;
sentences.n: ἔσσεται is ἔσεται ‘it shall be’, the future of εἰμί with a doubled σ (Attic ἔσται), and οὕτως is ‘so’. ἄττα is a respectful address from a younger man to an older one, ‘father’, with no family tie: Telemachus is speaking to Eumaeus.

sentences.t: σὺ δ’ ἔρχεο δειελιήσας·
sentences.tr: sy d’ ercheo deieliēsas·
sentences.l: and you go, having taken your evening meal;
sentences.i: and you, go once you have had your evening meal;
sentences.n: ἔρχεο is the imperative ‘go’. δειελιήσας is the aorist participle of δειελιάω, built on δείελος ‘late afternoon, evening’: ‘having dined at evening’ is the usual sense, but ‘having spent the evening’ is also given, and the exact meaning is not certain. Eumaeus does eat before he leaves (lines 602–603).

sentences.t: ἠῶθεν δ’ ἰέναι καὶ ἄγειν ἱερήϊα καλά·
sentences.tr: ēōthen d’ ienai kai agein hierēïa kala·
sentences.l: and at dawn to go and to bring fine victims;
sentences.i: and come at dawn, bringing fine victims;
sentences.n: ἰέναι ‘to go’ and ἄγειν ‘to bring’ are infinitives used as commands. ἠῶθεν is ‘at dawn’ (ending -θεν), and ἱερήϊα is ‘victims’ for sacrifice, with καλά ‘fine’. The Greek does not say what the sacrifice is for.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ τάδε πάντα καὶ ἀθανάτοισι μελήσει.
sentences.tr: autar emoi tade panta kai athanatoisi melēsei.
sentences.l: But to me these things all, and to the immortals, will be a care.”
sentences.i: But all this will be my concern, and the immortals’.”
sentences.n: αὐτάρ is ‘but’, ἐμοί ‘to me’, and τάδε πάντα ‘all these things’. ἀθανάτοισι is a dative plural in -οισι, ‘to the immortals’, the gods. μελήσει ‘will be a care’ is the future of the verb used in line 594.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάθ’, ὁ δ’ αὖτις ἄρ’ ἕζετ’ ἐϋξέστου ἐπὶ δίφρου,
πλησάμενος δ’ ἄρα θυμὸν ἐδητύος ἠδὲ ποτῆτος
βῆ ῥ’ ἴμεναι μεθ’ ὕας, λίπε δ’ ἕρκεά τε μέγαρόν τε,
πλεῖον δαιτυμόνων·
sentences.tr:
hōs phath’, ho d’ autis ar’ hezet’ eÿxestou epi diphrou,
plēsamenos d’ ara thymon edētyos ēde potētos
bē rh’ imenai meth’ hyas, lipe d’ herkea te megaron te,
pleion daitymonōn·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and he again then sat on the well-polished stool,
and having filled his heart with food and drink
he set out to go among the swine, and left the enclosures and the hall,
full of banqueters;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the swineherd sat down again on the well-polished stool, and when he had filled his heart with food and drink he set out for his swine, and left the courtyard and the hall, full of banqueters;
sentences.n: ὣς φάθ’ is ὣς ἔφατο ‘So he spoke’, with the vowel elided, and ὁ δ’ ‘and he’ turns back to Eumaeus; the English adds ‘the swineherd’ for clarity. ἕζετ’ is ἕζετο ‘sat down’, and ἐϋξέστου ‘well-polished’ goes with ἐπὶ δίφρου ‘on the stool’. πλησάμενος is the aorist middle participle of πίμπλημι ‘fill’, and ἐδητύος ἠδὲ ποτῆτος are genitives, ‘with food and drink’. βῆ ῥ’ ἴμεναι μεθ’ ὕας is ‘set out to go among the swine’ (ἴμεναι is an infinitive, ὕας the accusative plural of ὗς). λίπε is ‘left’, ἕρκεα ‘enclosures’, and πλεῖον ‘full’ takes the genitive δαιτυμόνων ‘of banqueters’.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ὀρχηστυῖ καὶ ἀοιδῇ
τέρποντ’·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ orchēstui kai aoidēi
terpont’·
sentences.l:
and they, with dancing and song,
took their delight;
sentences.i: while they took their pleasure in dancing and song;
sentences.n: οἱ δ’ ‘and they’ are the banqueters, the suitors. ὀρχηστυῖ and ἀοιδῇ are datives, ‘in dancing and song’. τέρποντ’ is τέρποντο ‘were taking delight’, the middle of τέρπω.

sentences.t: ἤδη γὰρ καὶ ἐπήλυθε δείελον ἦμαρ.
sentences.tr: ēdē gar kai epēlythe deielon ēmar.
sentences.l: for already indeed had come on the evening day.
sentences.i: for the evening of the day had already come on.
sentences.n: ἤδη γάρ is ‘for already’. ἐπήλυθε is the aorist of ἐπέρχομαι ‘come on, arrive’. δείελον ἦμαρ is ‘the evening day’, the day’s evening (δείελος ‘late afternoon, evening’, as in δειελιήσας at 599), and the line closes the part with the hour Odysseus asked to wait for.
